column2: Students and single faculty occupy the rooms on the 2nd and 3rd floors; couples, the Rices among them, take suites in the wings off the main corridor; families with small children settle into the cabins on the grounds. Lee Hall is searched for furniture, people wonder when classes will begin; the teachers pool their books in a small library; the first schedule is defined by meals. hunting for furniture, a shared library, meals as landmarks

Shortly after his arrival, Cramer, 18, meets his adviser Rice in one of the big green rocking chairs on the portico; Rice opens with a question about his interests; Cramer stammers that history is sort of fun; pressed to be more specific, he answers that he wants to know what caused the Depression; Rice laughs: “you have given the college a large order”; he steers him toward economics and history and also persuades him to try English composition and music, to the surprise of the former high-school athlete. green rocking chairs, a view of the clouds toward the peaks Consequences: Cramer specializes in recent American economic history

Shortly after Warburg's letter, Johnson writes to Barr: Albers is prepared to pay his own passage if necessary; Mrs. R. has given 500 dollars; Johnson declines any personal responsibility but judges that no better candidate can be found among the ex-Bauhäusler, useful for the industrial arts and typography. Barr, who had met Josef at the Dessau Bauhaus and had written him a long letter in German four years earlier, is in favor. $500 obtained from Mrs. R. (Rockefeller) Consequences: Barr's support secured

The group waits on the porch. A car arrives from the station, probably driven by Ted Dreier. The Alberses get out, oddly dressed, Juppi sporting a very strange haircut. They speak almost no English. Atmosphere: Amused, affectionate curiosity: “a pleasant picture to have in mind” Stakes: The meeting of two worlds — the Bauhaus lands in the Blue Ridge

With no routine and no program, the first days pass in turmoil; the Rollins people form a bloc, the outsiders wander about looking for classes; Martin discovers his neighbor Evarts, unshaven and consumed by doubt; no one knows which courses will exist. Words: McGraw: “complete state of bewilderment”; a non-Rollins student: “Those Who Had Been at Rollins were being confused with the Elect of God” Atmosphere: excitement mixed with fear in a small family where anonymity is impossible Stakes: creating a community even before a program

The community gathers on the vast columned porch facing the Blue Ridge Mountains; no pomp, no formal program, no speeches; Joseph Martin will forget even the statement of ideals; the occasion draws its effectiveness from its deliberate refusal of drama, and a certain flatness; it all ends with lunch. Words: Martin later writes that it was like an impromptu football game: they were there, and that was enough. Atmosphere: A splendid view of the mountains; a relaxed, deliberately unsolemn atmosphere. Stakes: The birth of a utopia without ceremony — the founding gesture lies in its refusal of ritual.

Georgia settles into the largest office and puts up the “president” sign; Rice, aghast, joins forces with Dreier to persuade him that the role is that of an educator among his peers; Georgia holds out for “president”; Rice proposes “rector,” which is accepted. Words: Georgia argues for “president”; Rice and Dreier plead for “chairman,” then “rector,” as an educator among equals Atmosphere: a muffled tug-of-war at the very beginning of the college Stakes: Who will embody the authority of the new college, and under what name

Rice, pipe in hand in a rocking chair facing the clouds over the peaks, opens with: what would he like to study? Cramer stammers that history is sort of fun; Rice narrows it down: which phase? The student, on the verge of panic, blurts out: what caused the Depression. Rice laughs, hails the large order placed with the college, steers him toward economics and history, and wrings out of him English composition and music. Words: “W-well, history is sort of fun” / “I want to know what caused the Depression” / “Well, you have given the college a large order!” Atmosphere: The serenity of the landscape against the student's nerves; the master's peaceful pipe smoking Stakes: A first encounter with Rice's Socratic teaching — and its two faces

At 9 a.m. one October day in 1933, Doughten Cramer and Frank Rice climb Craggy Dome (6,053 feet), guided by the directions of a farmer named Allen, one of the 31 members of the original community. They get lost, ask the way of a mountain man in front of a very dirty house with vicious dogs, follow Sugar Fork creek (crossed three times, its water drunk each time), reach the summit around 5 p.m., come down in less than an hour, meet a ranger and his companion who offer them food and company and invite them on a bear hunt, then walk in the dark, waking every dog in the valley, get a lift to Black Mountain, and reach the college at 9 p.m. Departure 9 a.m., lunch break 1:30 p.m., summit before 5 p.m., back at 9 p.m.; about 26 miles (~42 km) in all; a 3-hour climb, a descent of less than an hour; a trail like a continuous ladder at 45 degrees; silent woods, cold sunless stretches, then warm blackberry thickets; a rash of “No Trespassing” signs in the woods Consequences: A city boy's first real experience of the wilderness; two days later, ready to do it again

A public report exonerates Pace and condemns Hamilton Holt's actions at Rollins, in the aftermath of the conflict that led Rice and his colleagues to resign. Consequences: prepares Rice's rehabilitation

9 a.m.: departure. Lost, the two students come upon a dirty house besieged by dogs; Pa gives them outlandish directions. They find the road on the left, follow the tunnel-like trail, have lunch at 1:30 p.m., cross Sugar Fork three times drinking its water, climb a ladder at 45 degrees, reach the summit around 5 p.m. with a view all the way to the college building, a lightning descent, meet the ranger who feeds them royally and invites them on a bear hunt, walk at night amid the dogs of the whole valley, hitchhike to the college, arrive at 9 p.m., hot shower and sleep. Words: Pa: “You'll cross a stream called Sugar Fork three times while you skirt a cliff. Keep yourselves always to the right. But the first road you want to take will be on your left.” Atmosphere: The silence of the woods, the cold under the trees, the warmth of the brambles, the sweet ache of the water, mist at the summit, a night broken by barking Stakes: The city boy's initiation; the body pushed beyond itself; the mountain as an educator alongside the college

At a special meeting of the Board (Rice, Dreier, Georgia), those who had already been teaching for four or five weeks are officially elected members of the faculty: Evarts (music), Martin (English), Hinckley (psychology), Helen Boyden (economics), Hilda “Peggy” Loram (English and dramatics), Emmy Zastrow (German), and John Keith, recently arrived (Romance languages). The seven, like the three teachers on the Board, receive free room and board — but no salary. pay: free room and board, zero salary; in 1935-36 the average salary will be 819 dollars Consequences: a guiding principle described as a modified Marx: from each according to his abilities, to each according to his (meager) needs

Rice meets them at the station. From the start he is a little wary of Anni. His first judgment of Josef is enthusiastic (“Every now and then you meet a gracious German, and by God, it's wonderful!”). Rice's German is poor, and Albers knows almost no English despite a crash course during his last three weeks in Berlin; Anni, who had learned English as a child from her governess, serves as go-between. The three have a drink together, take a walk, and look at flowers. After half an hour, Rice is convinced: “I knew.” a three-week intensive English course in Berlin; a walk and flowers; a half-hour meeting Consequences: the beginning of the Alberses' presence at the college

For several weeks Emmy Zastrow had presided over a German table, and the students had rehearsed phrases of welcome — which they promptly forget when the Alberses climb the steps of Lee Hall. Anni realizes that Black Mountain, North Carolina, might just as well have been the Philippines. Looking up at the enormous Doric columns of the Lee Hall porch, she sees a photograph pinned to one of them with a thumbtack; it is explained to her that the columns are made of wood. Albers's first day: during the welcoming ceremony, he manages to say: “I want to open eyes.” A woman asks him his age; “forty-five”; she replies that he will never learn English, it is too late. wooden Doric columns; a thumbtack and a photograph; the opening sentence: “I want to open eyes” Consequences: Rice, furious at the woman's remark, tells her she has ruined Albers's interest in the language; Albers, thirty years later, will judge that she was right (“another flexibility of the mouth”)

Each receives a bedroom and bathroom in the side wing of Lee Hall (the faculty wing) and a studio in the main part; a separate wing houses the washrooms. Albers is delighted with the climate: better than in most places in America, cool in summer on the mountain, mild in winter. Ted Dreier confirms that people sleep under blankets all year round — “a nice assurance” of comfort. Twelve years at the Bauhaus have accustomed them to social experiment, but they believe in the need for privacy and in the distinction between the categories of teacher and student. individual bedrooms and bathrooms, studios, blankets all year round Consequences: they bring the college certainty, discipline, mastery of craft, well-defined personal styles, a refusal of idleness — controversial qualities

On Rice's motion, a committee studies the conditions of admission; its recommendations are adopted unanimously a month later: a personal interview with a representative of the college, a special examination for those who have not finished high school, a statement from the high-school principal or from a respectable person on the applicant's character and school record. Consequences: Duberman's criticism: the examination tests information, not vitality; the formal structure remained minimal and was circumvented

The month after his arrival, the Board of Fellows votes Albers a thousand dollars — the only formal salary on the faculty, funded by a special gift. $1,000, a special gift Consequences: the only salary among the teachers

Two months after the opening, Dreier draws up a projected budget: rent, light/heat/power including a driver's salary, food, scholarships, staff salaries; a total annual operating cost of about $32,000. rent $4,500; light/heat/power $4,200; food $7,000; scholarships $3,800; salaries $1,875 excluding Albers; secretary $135; a reserve of $1,000 for bad debts; a potential deficit of more than $8,000 at the end of the first year Consequences: constant fund-raising

Bulletin No. 1 puts a good face on the scarcity of books: the students have really benefited, since they see how useful a book is and how necessary it is to take the initiative in looking for information. BMC Bulletin No. 1, November 1933, Raleigh Archives

At Thanksgiving 1933, Wunsch unfortunately found students and teachers who hated Rollins and talked about it day after day; this negative attitude discouraged him, and salary was not the only reason for delaying his arrival. The following Thanksgiving, he found the college on its feet, engaged in a positive program; Rollins seemed forgotten; he was enthusiastic. Consequences: Wunsch finally joins the college

They dine with Ted Dreier's parents in Brooklyn Heights, where they meet “Aunt Kate” and Marcel Duchamp, whom Albers judges “a great fellow”. They visit the exhibition of Brancusi's sculptures organized by Duchamp and meet, among others, George Grosz (“sehr sympathisch”), their benefactors Philip Johnson and Edward M.M. Warburg, and the former Bauhaus student Werner Drewes. Albers's phrases: “a great fellow,” “sehr sympathisch”.

Thanks to the efforts of Ted Dreier's mother, the news of the arrival, stressing Josef's role as an educator, appears in all the major New York newspapers as well as in North Carolina. Albers writes to Perdekamp that there is a great deal of interest here and that people everywhere want to write about them.

On the first day, the secretary, a very healthy and appetizing girl, greets them on the porch; Anni notices her plump little pink toes in sandals and tells herself that maybe this is a true story after all — confirmation that freedom does reign here. Sandals; pink toes; porch.

Twelve teachers, some with young families, twenty-two idealistic students (thirteen of them transfers from Rollins College), and a handful of staff, including the African American couple Jack and Rubye Lipsey, who ran the kitchen and were highly regarded. 12 teachers, 22 students, 13 of them from Rollins

Josef and Anni Albers emigrate to the United States in November 1933; thanks to connections in New York and New England, a job offer reaches him even before he leaves Germany Consequences: He accepts a post at Black Mountain College and introduces there the teaching practices established in Dessau

Josef and Anni Albers arrive in the United States in November 1933 and travel directly from New York to Black Mountain College, where they will be based for sixteen years; in the summer of 1933, when he is approached in Berlin, Albers knows hardly any English but immediately sets about learning it, as a letter written from Berlin on September 21, 1933, to his friends Ludwig and Maud Grote in Dessau attests, in which he does not reveal the invitation he has received letter of September 21, 1933, to Ludwig and Maud Grote, Dessau Consequences: The beginning of sixteen years at Black Mountain College

Three students present to a community meeting the idea of a farm to save money and strengthen the community; after a long discussion, the proposal is adopted unanimously. a unanimous vote Consequences: The birth of the farm and a wider range of communal chores.

The AAUP report (Bulletin, Nov. 1933), despite some criticism of Rice, supports Rice and his sympathizers; a preliminary report was published on May 25, 1933. Bulletin of the AAUP, 19, pp. 416-39 Consequences: The founders of Black Mountain are legitimized
In November 1933, the Alberses sail for America. Albers, 45, leaves behind everything familiar to him. Consequences: Arrival at Black Mountain College.

Reporters are waiting for the Alberses on the docks; they are photographing the refugee Bauhaus art teacher when someone shouts “The wife. Let's get the wife, too”. Anni loved this moment of spontaneous friendliness. the reporters' shout Consequences: A first encounter with the American friendliness she learns to value

The preliminary report is made public at the end of May 1933; the official report appears in the AAUP Bulletin in November 1933: it clears Rice and censures Rollins, describing an excessive presidential authority, humiliating to the faculty and contrary to the bylaws. Furious, Holt wages a letter-writing campaign among academic colleagues for months, accuses the AAUP of bias, and in December 1933 publishes a special issue of the Rollins College Bulletin, sent to hundreds of leaders in academia, business, and government. Some reply sympathetically (William J. Hutchins of Berea), others ironically (Allan Gilbert of Duke). special issue of the Rollins College Bulletin, December 1933, 28 pages (3-28) Consequences: Rollins is threatened with removal from the AAUP's list of approved colleges
Josef and Anni leave Germany for good — for Black Mountain College, where they arrive at the opening. Consequences: The beginning of their American life and of Black Mountain

Press photographers snap away at the Bauhaus professor imported to the United States; someone shouts “Let's get the wife, too” — Anni is delighted and sees in it a sign of American kindness. In the photo, in a sealskin coat next to Josef in a top hat and overcoat, she looks dignified but not joyful. Johnson waits for them at the pier; the next day, he and Warburg take them to the latter's parents' home at 1109 Fifth Avenue (today the Jewish Museum, which holds Anni's Six Prayers) to see etchings by Rembrandt and Dürer, then to the Metropolitan, where the Alberses marvel at the eager crowds. Anni, excited by the new adventure, has few regrets about leaving Germany but feels guilty: her Jewishness, even more than the closure of the Bauhaus, forced Josef to leave his homeland; she calls herself a stone around his neck, a weight. Consequences: Two days later, they are at Black Mountain

A first shock: a thumbtack holds a notice to an Ionic column at Robert E. Lee Hall — unthinkable in Germany, where columns are made of marble; no notion of aristocracy. Where their German counterparts would go to take the waters at Baden-Baden or play baccarat, Ted and Bobbie Dreier go backpacking and join the road maintenance crew. Anni and Josef adapt quickly, Anni especially. a thumbtack on an Ionic column; backpacks instead of spa cures; a road crew instead of baccarat

The students, coached at Emmy Zastrow's German table, have rehearsed phrases of welcome that they forget as they climb the steps; Anni discovers the wooden Doric columns with a photo pinned to one; during the ceremony, Albers says “I want to open eyes”; a woman asks his age, “forty-five,” and declares that he will never learn English Words: “I want to open eyes” / “Then you will never learn English, it's too late” Atmosphere: warm and disconcerting, a collision of two worlds Stakes: the arrival of Europeans in the rural South; the initial linguistic wound

Visiting at Thanksgiving 1933, Wunsch finds students and teachers full of hatred for Rollins, talking about it day and night; discouraged, he delays his arrival; at Thanksgiving 1934, he finds the college on its feet, engaged in a positive program, Rollins forgotten Words: he found the college on its feet, actively engaged in a positive program; Rollins seemed forgotten; he was enthusiastic. Atmosphere: From disappointment to enthusiasm in a year Stakes: Can the college define itself other than against Rollins?

After the docking of the S.S. Europa (10 hours late, a hurricane), the Alberses dine at the home of Ted Dreier's parents, meet Aunt Kate and Duchamp, visit his Brancusi exhibition, and run into Grosz, their benefactors, and the former Bauhäusler Drewes. Words: Albers on Duchamp: “a great fellow”; on Grosz: “sehr sympathisch”. Atmosphere: A New York warming, the Thanksgiving weekend, an art world reaching out to the refugees Stakes: The old world (Duchamp, Grosz, Drewes) welcomes the survivors of the Bauhaus.

On the first day, the college secretary, a very healthy and appetizing girl, greets the couple on the porch, barefoot in sandals. Words: Anni, to herself: “Well maybe this is a true story”. Atmosphere: The height of American informality as seen by a Berliner; Southern light, a view of the Blue Ridge Stakes: Through a bodily detail, Anni gauges that the proclaimed freedom is real.

Three students propose creating a farm to save money and build the community; a long conversation, then a unanimous vote. Atmosphere: A long, lively debate before unanimity. Stakes: The institutional birth of the farm, a symbol of the community project.

The reporters snap away at the refugee professor; someone shouts to photograph the wife too; a moment Anni loved Words: the reporters' shout Atmosphere: flashbulbs, spontaneous American camaraderie Stakes: the welcome of the adopted country

On their arrival, the Alberses find a notice fastened with a thumbtack to an Ionic column Atmosphere: culture shock: in Germany columns are made of marble Stakes: America without an aristocracy: a first step in adapting

Photographers snap away at Josef; a shout: let's get the wife, too; Anni, delighted, sees American kindness in it; Johnson waits at the pier Words: “Let's get the wife, too” Atmosphere: flashbulbs, confused joy, a sealskin coat, a top hat Stakes: Anni accepts the role of the famous man's wife while keeping her reserved dignity

Typed minutes of the faculty meetings of November 7 and December 7, 1933; for the early years, these minutes, written by Mangold, say nothing at all except who was present and what actions were taken.

To enter into the ethos of the eighteenth century, the members staged Congreve's play. A stage was built by closing off part of the dining hall with curtains; rehearsals began in October. By Christmas, Rice, who was to take a part like all the members, still did not know his lines and refused, categorical and defiant, to learn them; Peggy Loram could not survive prolonged coaching; the play was performed before the half of the college that was not taking part, Rice carrying a prompt script rolled up like toilet paper. Curtains in the dining hall; a prompt script rolled up like toilet paper; prayers for Rice's memory. Consequences: A resounding success, a wild party after the curtain; the community saw it as an illustration of two convictions: the falseness of the distinction between curricular and extracurricular, and the central place of art.

At the same meeting, the faculty votes to encourage applicants to submit personal work (a poem, a story, a painting); on Peggy Loram's motion, “special students” may enroll in any course with the teacher's consent, without prerequisites. Unusual questions on the forms: if you do not intend to graduate, what is your plan? If your high-school grades are poor, how do you explain it?

Several students immediately fall behind in their fees; Dreier reports to the Board that it is unlikely that everything will be collected. fees set at $340 + $340 for room and board; $1,200 combined in the third year Consequences: a threat to the balance of the budget

Warburg, a trustee of the Museum of Modern Art, declares that Albers could fundamentally change the methods of art teaching in this country; his main interest is to draw out his students' creative possibilities through experimental exercises in technique.

At the welcoming ceremony, asked what he hoped to accomplish in the United States, Albers, gathering his meager English, answers simply: “I want to open eyes”. The article presents him as internationally known for his unusual method of teaching art. Consequences: A formula that sums up his teaching: opening vision, training an audience for abstraction

Rehearsals since October; at Christmas Rice still does not know his lines and refuses, categorical and defiant, to learn them; Loram on the verge of collapse; last-minute touch-ups, prayers for Rice's memory, the performance before half the college; Rice paces the stage with his prompt script rolled up like toilet paper; triumph and a wild party. Atmosphere: Collective farce, comic suspense, final euphoria. Stakes: Does the founder refuse to learn, or is he testing the community? Art at the center against the vanity of the role.

The couple, newly arrived from Germany, is welcomed; Josef is asked what he hopes to accomplish in the United States; he gathers his little English and answers simply “I want to open eyes” Words: “I want to open eyes” Atmosphere: The emotion of a providential exile, the tension of recent immigrants Stakes: What the Bauhaus brings to America, condensed into a single sentence

The Cuban designer Clara Porset, trained in New York and Paris in the twenties and interested in the Bauhaus approach, traveled from Havana to Black Mountain to discover Josef's teaching, and was won over; she at once invited the couple to Cuba. Porset wrote that Albers teaches with the prodigality of one who possesses an inexhaustible treasure (article in Ahora, late December 1934-early January 1935) Consequences: The couple's first Latin American trip, December 1934
Josef Albers takes several portraits of Clara Porset during a visit to Havana. Several photographs preserved Consequences: The beginning of the relationship with Porset

Josef makes the art courses the center of the curriculum. Anni returns to weaving and, in the fall, joins the faculty and develops a complex new theoretical and teaching program for the weaving workshop.

The Cuban designer and architect, trained in New York and Paris in the 1920s, wanted to learn about the Bauhaus approach to design and contacts Josef soon after his arrival in the United States; she travels from Havana to Black Mountain to experience his teaching at first hand and is not disappointed. Consequences: She immediately invites Josef and Anni to Cuba

Josef places the art courses at the center of education at BMC; Anni rejoins the faculty in the fall and works out a theoretical and teaching program for the weaving workshop. Invited by the Cuban designer Clara Porset (who arrived at BMC in September), Josef gives a three-day series of lectures at the Lyceum in Havana (a women's club founded in 1928, later merged with the Lawn Tennis Club). The Alberses travel in the Dreiers' car with Ted and Bobbie. trip 1934-12-28 – 1935-01-16; letter to the Gropiuses of January 22, 1935: coffee, beans, black cigarettes, real rum

“Last year” (relative to 1935), the students took over the running of the farm on their own; during the summer, some stay on in rotation to prepare the crops, which the whole college harvests in the fall, without conflict with the academic calendar. Summer rotations; a collective fall harvest; an economic benefit for the college Consequences: A model of collective tasks replacing the artificial sports of other schools

Rice soon regrets having made Georgia rector: he thinks Georgia does not understand the wish that the head should not really be the head and would like to invest the office with more authority. Georgia gladly hands the office over to Rice after a year, to Rice's mild surprise; this readiness shakes his subconscious belief in demonology. It remains to be seen whether Rice will be able to stick to the idea of a purely ceremonial rectorship.

As early as the spring of the first year, formal amendments to the bylaws give every member of the college the right to inspect all the records of the corporation, recognize the student body's right to adopt a constitution for its own government, guarantee student representatives the right to attend and speak at regular faculty meetings, and give the Student Moderator a voting seat on the Board of Fellows. Dreier had announced publicly that no important decision affecting the students would be made without consulting them. Consequences: student representation greater than at most colleges, but not equality: Rice admits that some (the fellows) are more equal than others

After a visit in 1934 to the Lincoln School, a bastion of progressive education, Rice finds the place almost lifeless, running on something that happened long ago; a damning verdict: progressive education, when it is stupid, is far stupider than the other kind. Consequences: reinforces BMC's educational antidogmatism

Every summer, the Protestant Blue Ridge Assembly takes back its buildings for its conferences; a few members of the college stay on to handle day-to-day affairs. In the second year, these are Fred Mangold (instructor in modern languages) and his wife Isabel. Mangold describes a convention of nine hundred vegetarian cretins, all Seventh-day Adventists; a Christian dies after an afternoon of baseball in the sun followed by a plunge into the lake; the castration of the farmer's pig; sniggering YMCA secretaries Consequences: Ironic bulletins sent to the scattered members of the college

A long passage of the diary written at the end of the first year: John was in love with “Paul” in spite of himself, in spite of his attachment to someone else in New York; he confessed his affection to him, which embarrassed Paul and shocked him by its lack of reserve; then “Ann” and Paul began to weave a web around them.

End of the college's first year: John, in love with “Paul” in spite of himself (devoted to someone else in New York), declares his affection to him; Paul is embarrassed, shocked by the lack of reserve; “Ann” and Paul then grow close, John avoids Paul, Ann mocks his “self-dramatization”; in this closed world, the episode is visible to the whole community. John polite if he runs into Paul; salt in a wound; work more depressing than ever Consequences: John falls in the group's esteem

Rice gets John to talk about what is upsetting him, sees the situation as it is, then sets out to him the seriousness of the insinuations and criticisms aroused, shattering John's regained confidence. Rice breaks John's new confidence Consequences: John clings to his friends up north and to the feeling of having tried everything for the college

Second year: students open a cooperative store, open briefly each day; the college sets up its print shop; library shelving, looms, and furniture are built; a “Cottage School” for young children (the older ones attend school in the village) is run by students and attended for a time by children from the town. sales of cigarettes, paper, candy bars, instant cocoa; accounts chronically out of balance; the town children withdraw when “evolution” is discussed Consequences: attempts at self-sufficiency

Since Wunsch refuses room and board alone (he must support his mother and sister), the students collect a thousand dollars for his salary; part of the faculty, living on pennies, resents it; an inconclusive general meeting. 1000 dollars; Rice adjourns the meeting: “there's no consensus here”; he advises the students to go and persuade the opponents. Consequences: Wunsch finally receives his invitation.

First day: Dewey slightly disappoints the community because he does not visibly enthuse like previous visitors; he observes quietly, gently discourages being treated as a Great Philosopher, attends Rice's class every day, wanders about unobtrusively, and drinks beer with the students in the evening. Another visit during 1934-1935 brings with him Albert Barnes, the art collector. Every evening before dinner, whiskey with Dewey and two or three others, supplied by Barnes (a whole case of divine whiskey, according to Rice) Consequences: After his second visit, Dewey agrees to sit on the college's Advisory Council

Before the college is six months old, Wilder, invited by John Evarts, whom he knew at Yale, wins the college over: dinners with the students, endless questions, anecdotes about the famous (Elinor Wylie, Spengler, the Lunts, Woolcott, Ruth Gordon, Katharine Hepburn), evenings reading his one-act plays before the big fireplace in the Lee Hall lobby, an evening at the Dreiers' cottage with the Alberses and Evarts (conversation alternating between German and English), a public lecture, and a final talk with Rice. He buys a woodcut from Albers for 10 dollars (a special price), and Albers adds a second as a gift; he leaves 25 dollars for the library fund; 250 outside guests at the lecture Consequences: Wilder promises to try to come back in the spring (Rice had offered him one semester of teaching a year); compliments the emotional climate but suggests more human diversity and a little more intellectual discipline

In his capacity as rector, Georgia reminds the community that it will be judged by the quality of the intellectual work accomplished; the past year has produced some, but far from what the group is capable of; without notable progress, the college would lose much of its reason for being. Consequences: An affirmation of the centrality of academic work

Bulletin No. 2 (1934), translated from the German by Ted Dreier, who went over every shade of meaning of every sentence with Albers every evening for a month. a month of evenings of translation Consequences: a major text on Albers's teaching

Albers delivers a text setting out his material exercises and their rationale: optical and tactile perception, the primal need to touch materials. Consequences: Lays the theoretical foundation of the material studies at BMC.

Albers publishes in the Black Mountain College Bulletin an essay setting out the logic of his teaching of drawing: drawing as a visual language, expressive drawing excluded at the start, elementary teaching as a strictly objective craft. Consequences: this text sets the fundamental themes of his drawing course

In the early years of the color course at Black Mountain, Albers devotes the first sessions to the known color systems; later (at Yale), he saves them for the last week of the course, an island of theory in a course that celebrates empirical observation. Goethe's triangle, Schopenhauer's wheel, Runge's sphere, the systems of Albert Munsell and Wilhelm Ostwald.

In the year after his arrival, Albers publishes a statement: after the basic studies (drawing, design, color), which take half a year, there is no hurry to start painting; studies from nature or from the model concern the relations among color, form, and space. He cites Rembrandt, who at thirty is said to have felt the need for twenty years of study for a problem of color and space. Consequences: Reveals the apprehensions of a teacher obliged to build a course while training himself.

Approached on Albers's behalf by Edward Warburg of MoMA, Sawyer, the director of the gallery, agrees to show a group of Albers's prints. Consequences: Albers's first recognition in New England; Sawyer will later recruit him to Yale
Albers publishes his text on art teaching in the college Bulletin; in it he tells an anecdote about Rembrandt.
A student in the color course at Black Mountain poses in front of a blackboard bearing a color wheel; photograph preserved in the North Carolina State Archives. a color wheel drawn on the blackboard

Every day is structured by chores except Saturday, devoted to Japanese school, where the children discover calligraphy. At eight, Asawa describes the movement of the brush as a dance. “It was like a dance. Lift your feet up and lift your hands.”

The circular seal with concentric patterns symbolizes, according to Albers, “coming together, standing together, working together”. It strongly resembles Gropius's diagram of the Bauhaus curriculum, but without a prescriptive program. a round medallion, a concentric design Consequences: An emblem of the mutual relationship between individual and community

The Alberses cross Florida with their new friends Theodore and Barbara Dreier (among the founders of Black Mountain and housemates of the Alberses), on their way to a lecture in Havana; Anni has the idea of a trip to Mexico the following year. Consequences: The plan for the first Mexican trip

On the eve of leaving for the national convention of letter carriers in Cleveland, for which he had long been preparing, the father asks to borrow his son's suitcase, bigger and newer than his own; Olson, about 24, refuses without giving a reason. Consequences: The father leaves angry; shortly afterward he is hospitalized and dies in August 1935 (heart); to the end he refused to speak to his son or to acknowledge his presence during his visits.
Albers publishes woodcuts and linocuts in Asheville in 1934, probably prepared through drawings that do not seem to have survived.
In the college's second year, Rice becomes rector and Georgia takes the post of secretary.

Albers despairs at the lack of formality in faculty and Board of Fellows meetings: he wanted a strict agenda known in advance; Rice let the faculty come in, sit down, and talk about whatever came up. Albers judged Rice totally undisciplined. Consequences: a lasting tension of style between the two men

A hired farmer helps produce about half the vegetables eaten in the dining hall. Attempts at raising pigeons, the apple harvest, hauling coal from the Black Mountain station in the college pickup, an attempt at a campus store. 50% of the vegetables; coal unloaded by hand

De Kooning embarks on his first abstract compositions, then destroys most of them by painting over them; only those that meet his demand for a new masterpiece escape his merciless self-criticism. Consequences: A reputation as an artist unable to finish his paintings.
Becomes a member of the Artists' Union.

At the request of the architect Philip Johnson, Josef Albers designs the cover of the catalog of MoMA's Machine Art exhibition, with a dramatic photograph of an industrial ball bearing. The printer's first proofs do not respect his margins; Albers rejects them and demands that his name as designer be removed if the defect is not corrected. the required margin between the edge of the paper and the image: exactly three millimeters; image: a gleaming industrial ball bearing Consequences: Johnson replies contritely and promises to bring the margin back to three millimeters in accordance with the original design

With Maxwell Fry's help, the Gropiuses settle in England. Many think he was fleeing as much to get Ise away from Herbert Bayer as to escape the Nazis — the same motive as when he left the Bauhaus six years earlier.

The measles he contracted in 1934 leads to scleroderma, a disease of the mucous membranes that slowly kills him without preventing an extraordinary late body of work in which war and death replace birth and the splendors of nature. Consequences: Death in July 1940, less than a year after his 60th birthday

Mies is “provoked” (Johnson's word) by the reproduction of his furniture without credit; Johnson puts the blame on House & Garden magazine, which did not use the information supplied, and denies having taken the credit, mentioning furniture made as well for his friend Edward M. M. Warburg. House & Garden magazine; Johnson's clarification that he is including a Brno chair in an exhibition at the Modern, “proudly attributed” to Mies Consequences: The beginning of Johnson's later antipathy toward Mies.

Four years after leaving Germany, Hofmann opens a school in New York that attracts students from all over the country; he teaches there two grueling days a week (morning, afternoon, and evening classes). Two days a week; morning, afternoon, and evening classes; sometimes seventy people in class for demonstrations. Consequences: Hofmann becomes one of the most influential art teachers of his generation.

Between January and early April 1934, an extensive correspondence among Mrs. Joseph Swan (a former trustee of Bennington and an acquaintance of Johnson's), Johnson, Albers, and President Robert Leigh, with a view to an appointment of Albers at Bennington for 1934-35. Albers's BMC contract expiring on June 12, 1934; uncertainty about BMC's solvency; a wish to be closer to New York Consequences: Bennington's final refusal; Albers stays at Black Mountain until 1949

John conveys his strong affection to Paul; embarrassment, shock; Ann and Paul close in on themselves; Paul becomes distant; John avoids Paul but stays polite; Ann needles John with sarcasm; all of it before the eyes of the whole college Words: Ann mocks John's self-dramatization Atmosphere: claustrophobic — our little universe, where it is impossible to avoid one another; salt in a wound Stakes: forbidden love in a glass village

Rice brings up John's work, gets him to talk, sees the situation clearly, then sets out to him the seriousness of the group's insinuations and criticisms Words: Rice stresses the seriousness of the insinuations Atmosphere: briefly liberating, then destructive Stakes: the founder, ally and censor

The students have raised 1000 dollars; an inconclusive meeting; Rice adjourns for lack of consensus; the bewildered students come to see him; he sends them back to persuade the opponents. Words: Rice: “there's no consensus here”; “If I was running the show—but I'm not running this show, because it's yours”. Atmosphere: The resentment of the underpaid faculty at the thousand dollars. Stakes: Who governs: the community or its agents.

Conversation alternating between German and English: Wilder's schooling in China, Mary Pickford's plan for a play with him, Goethe's theory of colors, Wilder's trick for remembering telephone numbers by their melody, Kandinsky's art, Gene Tunney. Afterward Wilder buys a print from Albers for 10 dollars, and Albers gives him a second. Words: The Alberses on Wilder: “Ein fabelhafter Kerl! So lebendig—so kraftvoll und tuend—er ist ein richtiger moderner Mensch!!” Atmosphere: Warm, brilliant, bilingual Stakes: The New York literary world meets the refugees of the Bauhaus

Wilder gives a lecture on the relations between literature and life before the whole college and 250 guests; he flatters local pride (experimental colleges) and national pride (America holds the new subject: the multitude), without guaranteeing a Renaissance; afterward a pert-pussied Asheville matron invites him to spend Saturday at her house in Biltmore Forest. Words: America has its hands on a new subject — the multitude — but one cannot be sure it is turning the corner toward a great Renaissance Atmosphere: A large audience, society

Before leaving, Wilder tells Rice of his enthusiasm for the emotional climate (a mysteriously happy atmosphere) but expresses reservations: too few people and too few kinds of people, and a little more intellectual discipline would do no harm. Rice offers him one semester of teaching a year; Wilder replies diplomatically that he will try to come back in the spring and leaves 25 dollars for the library. Words: a mysteriously happy atmosphere; a little more intellectual discipline Atmosphere: Frank, courteous Stakes: The first lucid outside assessment of the project
